coherence.reasons: Both documents run a clean line from governing thought to recommendation, and both governing thoughts carry the key condition (payback only if ad cost stays near the pilot's 28%). X's whether / route / how structure maps one-to-one onto its slides, and its hypothesis-test slide (four conditions, each with a verdict) ties every section back to the answer. Its gate thresholds are derived from its own model: 28% from the 28.6% break-even, 34% from zero 2029 operating profit. Y's five-section structure also mirrors its executive summary, but it has small internal slips. Slide 18 says three pilot numbers (ad cost, repeat, labels) 'become the launch gates', yet the recommendation gates only ad cost and awareness. Slide 14 switches to cumulative operating profit to claim Japan earns more 'only' at 32% ACoS, while Y's own slide 13 shows Japan ahead on cash at 28% ($1.8M vs $0.4M). X's one tension, recommending A while showing payback is likely missed at benchmark ACoS, is resolved explicitly by asking the board to pre-agree the slip.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred conclusion: Amazon-led with gates, retail earned at 20% awareness or more plus a door test, the $40M ambition reset, and Japan as fallback. X weighs the trade-offs more fully and more honestly. It concedes that Japan yields more four-year cash unless US ACoS stays below about 26%, and argues for the US on what it builds rather than on near-term cash. It considers and rejects waiting a year. It treats a payback slip in the amber case as a departure from a board limit that the board must decide in advance. Its green / amber / red gates have derived thresholds, defined responses, a volume trigger and a tariff adjustment, and it sizes exposure at Gate 1 ($1.9–2.9M). Y's judgment is sound but thinner. It has a single 28% gate 'after 12 months' with a softer consequence ('hold SKU and ad expansion'). It never says that at the likely 32% benchmark the board's payback rule is breached and what the board should do about it. It understates how close the Japan trade-off is.

evidence.reasons: Both reproduce the key's numbers accurately: about $10.73 before ads, $4.01 at 28% ACoS, retail $7.55, Option B peak −$20.8M, 4.5% group margin in 2027, Option A at +$2.40M / +$0.38M / −$2.32M, and a 28.6% break-even. Both handle the $5.2B figure and the 0.71 correlation correctly, cite the Mooncrest loss, and note that two of three Amazon-first entrants stalled. X goes further and stays accurate. It gives CAGRs of 17.3% vs 5.1%, a 6×4 ACoS-by-volume grid, ten stress cases with peak cash and margin, and a stall case modelled on Gaon Lab and Yeoreum. It shows what B would need to pay back (a 3.1× halo or 23.5 units per door per week), B at realistic inputs (−$26.4M), a doors-to-break-even figure (about 4,250), and FX and tariff sensitivities. It also has an explicit list of judgement calls. Y adds a few useful touches: the pilot-plus-tariff case (−$0.63M), the lower-quartile 3.9 point that justifies a door test even above 20% awareness, and the 39% share of category growth. But Y makes some unsupported or misleading claims. 'Japan earns more only if US ad cost runs at 32%' holds only on operating profit before inventory; on cash, Japan is ahead at 28%. 'Every repeat order is a sale with little or no ad cost' and the claim that TikTok brings sales Onsoo does not pay Amazon for are not in the pack. 'Korea shows the formula can earn far more loyalty' leans toward the Korean-repeat trap, though Y hedges it. X's weakest inference is the extrapolation to $40M by about 2032 at 29% growth, which it flags as conditional.

revision.reasons: Both handle the CEO's hypothesis as the key expects: keep Amazon-first, add an ad-cost gate, raise the retail awareness trigger from 15% to 20% with a door test (because the 10–20% band's 3.5 median is below the 4.0 delisting line), and reset the $40M timing. X is more rigorous. It breaks the hypothesis into four testable conditions with explicit verdicts: two hold, one holds only if ACoS is 28.6% or lower, and the 2029 retail trigger does not hold. It then states a revised answer, turning the dated 2029 retail step into an earned option and measuring the halo rather than assuming it. Y's side-by-side table of the CEO's plan against the recommended plan is clear and reaches the same substantive revisions. It is less explicit that the payback condition is likely to fail at benchmark ACoS, and that this changes what the board is being asked to approve.

overall.reasons: Both documents are defensible and numerically sound, and both meet all four of the key's defensibility criteria. X serves the board better in three ways. It names the real decision: the route probably misses the 2030 payback at benchmark ad costs, so the board must decide in advance whether a slip is acceptable. It bounds the downside across many cases (peak cash of $7.2M or less, group margin of 8.8% or more). It gives operational gates with derived thresholds and defined responses. It is also more candid that Japan beats the US on four-year cash unless ACoS stays below about 26%. Y is tighter and reaches the same conclusion with correct core numbers, but it softens the Japan comparison by switching metric, includes a few unsupported claims, and offers a thinner gate mechanism.
